parts: When the red phone box at the end of Elm Street stopped working, most people in the village of Hadley hardly noticed. Everyone had a mobile, and the box had been empty for years, apart from the occasional spider. But fifteen-year-old Maya Collins walked past it every morning on her way to the bus stop, and she had an idea.

“My gran always said that a village without a library is like a kitchen without a kettle,” Maya explains. “Our library closed when I was ten, and the nearest one is forty minutes away by bus. I thought: why not put some shelves in the phone box and fill them with books?”

Getting permission was harder than she expected. The phone company still owned the box, and at first nobody answered her emails. In the end, she asked her head teacher for help, and the school wrote a letter on her behalf. Two months later, the village council bought the box for just one pound.

Maya’s dad, who is a carpenter, built three narrow shelves, and her friends painted a sign. Then came the most important part: the books. Maya put a notice in the village shop asking for donations, and within a week she had more than three hundred – far too many for such a tiny space. “We keep the extra ones in our garage,” she laughs. “My mum isn’t very happy about that.”

The rules are simple: take a book, bring a book, or just take one if you have nothing to bring. There is no library card and no fine for late returns. Some people were worried that the books would disappear, but that hasn’t happened. In fact, the shelves are often fuller at the end of the week than at the beginning.

What surprised Maya most was who uses it. “I thought it would be mainly children,” she says, “but lots of older people come, and they stop and chat. One man told me he hadn’t spoken to his neighbour for years, and now they swap detective stories every Friday.”
Maya is now planning a children’s corner and a notebook where readers can recommend books to each other. And the spiders? “They’ve moved out,” she says. “I think they prefer the garage.”

For most of us, boredom is something to be avoided at all costs. The moment we find ourselves waiting for a bus or standing in a queue, out comes the phone. Yet a growing number of psychologists believe that by filling every empty moment, we may be losing something valuable.

In one well-known experiment, a researcher asked a group of volunteers to copy numbers from a telephone directory for fifteen minutes – a task deliberately designed to be as dull as possible. Then both groups were asked to think of as many uses as they could for a pair of plastic cups.

The results were striking. The volunteers who had been bored came up with more ideas, and more original ones, than those who had not. When the mind has nothing interesting to focus on, it seems, it starts to wander, and this daydreaming allows it to make unexpected connections.

This would not have surprised many famous writers and inventors, who often describe their best ideas arriving at moments of apparent idleness – on long walks, in the bath or while staring out of a train window. Their problem was rarely a lack of time to think; if anything, they had plenty of it.

For children, the argument may be even more important. Many parents feel guilty if their son or daughter complains of having nothing to do, and rush to organise another activity. Educational experts, however, suggest that resisting this urge can help children develop independence, imagination and the ability to entertain themselves.

None of this means that we should deliberately make our lives as boring as possible. Long-lasting boredom, the kind that continues for weeks or months, is linked to low mood and can be a sign that something needs to change. Next time you are waiting for a bus, you might try leaving your phone in your pocket. You never know what you might think of.
A. Marta, from lawyer to baker.

For eleven years I worked in corporate law, and by any objective measure I was successful. What I hadn’t anticipated was how little of it I would remember: whole years blurred into a sequence of deadlines. Baking had always been my way of switching off, so when a friend asked me to supply cakes for her café, I agreed almost as a joke. Within six months the orders had outgrown my kitchen. The financial drop was brutal – I earn perhaps a third of what I used to – and I won’t pretend I never lie awake doing sums. But I can point to something at the end of every day and say: I made that. My former colleagues tend to assume I had some kind of breakdown. I didn’t. I simply looked hard at my own life and didn’t like what I saw.
B. Daniel, from engineer to teacher.

I didn’t so much leave engineering as drift out of it. I’d been mentoring graduates for years and realised it was the part of the week I looked forward to. Retraining as a physics teacher at forty-three was humbling: my first observed lesson was, frankly, a disaster. What nobody tells you is how physically exhausting teaching is – I was asleep by nine for the whole of my first term. Still, I’d do it again tomorrow. When a fifteen-year-old asks what the point of equations is, I can describe a bridge I helped to design, and suddenly the maths has a purpose. I do occasionally miss the problem-solving, though – that particular satisfaction of making a design actually work.
C. Priya, from journalist to software developer.

Newspapers were shrinking around me, and after the third round of redundancies I decided to jump before I was pushed. I chose coding largely for practical reasons: there were jobs, and the courses were short. I’d assumed the two worlds had nothing in common, but they’re remarkably alike – both reward clarity and punish vagueness, and both involve explaining complicated things to people who would rather not think about them. The course itself was intense and, at times, demoralising. What kept me going was a mentor who insisted that asking basic questions was a strength rather than an admission of failure. Two years on, I earn more than I ever did as a reporter, which still feels faintly absurd.
D. Stephen, from police officer to city guide.

After thirty years in the police, retirement was supposed to mean golf. It lasted about four months. I’d always been the colleague who knew the history of every street we patrolled, so becoming a city guide felt like a natural extension of something I’d done informally for decades. The qualification took longer than I’d imagined – there’s a written exam and a practical assessment, and I failed the practical the first time because I talked too much and lost half the group. The pay is modest and irregular; I couldn’t live on it without my pension. But I’ve never been less stressed. People on a tour have chosen to be there, which is a pleasant change from my previous line of work, where nobody was ever pleased to see me.

Our indoor wall is open on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Beginners are welcome, and all equipment is included in the price. Instructors stay with you the whole time, so it’s safe even if you’ve never climbed before.
Every Saturday morning we cook a three-course meal together and then eat it! You’ll learn dishes from a different country each month. Bring an apron – we provide the ingredients.
Write, film and edit your own short films using only a phone. At the end of term, the best films are shown at the town cinema. Meetings on Wednesday afternoons.
Quiet games every Monday after school in the library. Players of all levels meet to play and learn new strategies. There’s a friendly tournament once a month, but nobody has to take part.
We look after the community garden and grow vegetables that we give to local families. Most of the work is outdoors on Friday afternoons, so wear old clothes!
Rehearsals on Tuesdays and Thursdays for our big summer show. Everyone gets a speaking part, and you’ll perform on a real stage in front of hundreds of people.
Long walks in the hills every Sunday, with a picnic lunch. You need good shoes and a reasonable level of fitness, as some walks are over fifteen kilometres.
Learn to build simple games and apps. We meet on Wednesday evenings in the computer room, and you can work alone or in small teams. No experience needed.

Last spring, I was going to visit my cousin in Bristol for the weekend. I had never travelled alone by train before, so I was a bit nervous. My mum came with me to the station and helped me find the right platform.

I found a seat by the window, put on my headphones and started reading a book. The train was quiet and comfortable, and after a while I fell asleep. Outside the window there were mountains, and I was sure there were no mountains between London and Bristol.

I went to find the ticket inspector. When I showed her my ticket, she looked at it for a long time. I had got on the right train, but at the next station it had divided into two parts, and I was in the part going north!
The inspector was very kind. She told me to get off at the next stop and wait for a train back. My cousin wasn’t worried at all – in fact, she laughed so much that she couldn’t speak for a minute.
I finally arrived in Bristol four hours late, tired and hungry. Now, every time I take a train, I check the signs on the doors very carefully, and I never fall asleep.

Every October, thousands of people queue for hours and pay good money to be chased through dark corridors by actors dressed as zombies. Horror films regularly top the box office, and roller coasters keep getting taller. At first sight, it makes little sense: fear evolved to keep us away from danger, so why would anyone go looking for it?

Part of the answer lies in what happens in the body. When we are frightened, the brain releases a rush of adrenaline and other chemicals that sharpen the senses and prepare us to fight or run. In a genuinely dangerous situation, that feeling is deeply unpleasant. But when we know, at some level, that we are safe, the same physical reaction can be experienced as excitement – even joy. Researchers who interviewed visitors leaving a haunted house found that many felt calmer and happier afterwards than before they went in.

The key, psychologists say, is control. A horror film can be paused; a scary attraction has an exit. We are, in effect, choosing to experience a strong emotion within clear limits. Some experts compare it to play-fighting among young animals: a way of rehearsing how to react to a threat without facing any real risk. People who regularly watch frightening films, one study suggested, coped slightly better with anxiety during a period of real-world uncertainty.

There is also a social side. Being scared together creates a powerful sense of connection. Friends who scream on the same ride often feel closer afterwards, and couples on a first date may confuse the racing heart caused by a horror film with romantic attraction – a phenomenon that cinemas have quietly profited from for decades.

Not everyone, of course, enjoys the experience. For some people, the line between pleasant excitement and genuine distress is very thin, and personality, past experiences and even mood on the day can make the difference. The thrill also depends on getting the dose right: too little fear and we are bored; too much and we simply want to leave. Designers of scary attractions spend a great deal of time trying to find that balance.
So next time a friend suggests a horror film, you might think of it less as a strange taste and more as a form of training – a safe rehearsal for the moments in life when the fear is real.

The idea came from my own wardrobe: it was full of things I’d worn twice. I built the first version of the app with a friend from my coding course, and for months we did everything ourselves, from customer service to packaging. What I underestimated was how lonely it can be. When things go wrong at two in the morning, there’s no manager to call. These days we have twelve employees, and the thing I’m proudest of isn’t the sales figures – it’s that people actually enjoy working here.

I never planned to have a business. I fixed bikes for neighbours as a teenager, and word spread. When the local bike shop closed, people started knocking on my door, so I rented a garage and made it official. My parents were nervous – they wanted me to go to university – and I understand why. The money was terrible for the first two years. But I’ve never once woken up dreading the day, and I don’t think many of my friends can say that.

We raised a lot of investment very quickly, which sounds like a dream but put enormous pressure on us. Investors wanted growth, and we grew too fast, hiring people before we really knew what they would do. We nearly ran out of money in our third year. Looking back, it was the best lesson I could have had: now I question every expense. If I could give one piece of advice, it would be to grow slowly and never be embarrassed to ask for help.

People assume I had rich parents, but I started with my savings from a summer job and a borrowed kitchen. The first batches were a disaster – one even caught fire. What saved us was a small shop owner who agreed to sell our snacks and gave us brutally honest feedback every week. We changed the recipe eleven times. Now we’re in supermarkets across the country, but I still visit that first shop every month.

It has become something of a ritual for commentators to lament the death of reading. Yet by most measures we read more words today than at any time in history: messages, headlines, captions, threads. What has changed is not the quantity but the texture of our reading. We skim, we scan, we hop from link to link, and the long, uninterrupted engagement with a single text – once the default – now feels almost like an act of resistance.

Researchers who study reading on screens have noticed a pattern they describe, rather unkindly, as ‘F-shaped’: the eye moves across the first lines, drops down the left-hand side and picks up the occasional phrase. This is an efficient strategy for extracting information from a web page. The trouble begins when the habit migrates to texts that were never designed to be read that way – a novel, a closely argued essay, a contract. Comprehension of detail, studies suggest, suffers most when readers are under the impression that they have understood perfectly well.

Advocates of what has come to be called ‘slow reading’ are careful not to present it as a nostalgic rejection of technology. Their argument is subtler: that deep reading is a skill, and like any skill it weakens with neglect. The cognitive scientist Maryanne Wolf has written about her own unsettling discovery, after years of online reading, that she could no longer settle into a novel she had once loved; she had to retrain herself, page by reluctant page, over the following weeks.

What exactly is lost? Not simply information, its defenders argue, but a particular kind of thinking. Sustained reading obliges us to hold an argument in mind, to notice when it contradicts itself, to tolerate ambiguity long enough for meaning to emerge. Fiction, in particular, invites us to inhabit perspectives other than our own – a capacity some researchers link, cautiously, to empathy. These are not luxuries; they are precisely the capacities a democracy depends on.

None of this means abandoning screens, which are, after all, simply surfaces. A long article can be read slowly on a tablet, and a printed book can be skimmed. The real variable is attention, and attention is shaped by environment: notifications, open tabs, the faint itch to check something. Many slow readers report that the most effective change they made was not technological but spatial – a chair, an hour, a phone in another room.

Perhaps the most persuasive case for slow reading is also the least measurable. Those who rediscover it often describe not an improvement in productivity but something closer to relief: the pleasure of being absorbed, of losing track of time, of a mind no longer pulled in several directions at once. In an economy that competes ferociously for our attention, choosing where to give it may be one of the few freedoms we still fully control.

For much of the twentieth century, cities were designed around a single, unquestioned assumption: that the future belonged to the car. Streets were widened, pavements narrowed and whole neighbourhoods divided by motorways. Today, a growing number of planners argue that this vision was not merely unattractive but economically and socially costly.

The case for ‘walkable’ cities rests partly on health. People who live in neighbourhoods where shops, schools and parks are within a short walk tend to be more active, often without deliberately exercising at all. Over a population, small differences in daily movement add up to significant reductions in illnesses linked to inactivity.

There is an economic argument too, and it surprises many shopkeepers. Studies in several European cities have found the opposite: pedestrians may spend less per visit than drivers, but they visit more often, and over a month they tend to spend more.

Perhaps the most interesting findings, however, concern something harder to measure. Streets where people walk are streets where people meet – a neighbour at the bakery, a colleague at a crossing. Urban researchers have documented how residents of streets with heavy traffic report fewer friends among their neighbours than those living on quieter roads nearby.

None of this is to suggest that cars can or should be banished. The most successful schemes have tended to proceed gradually, often beginning with temporary changes – a closed road on Sundays, a few planters and benches – that residents can try before anything permanent is built.

Paris, Barcelona and Ljubljana are often cited as examples, but the principle is modest enough to apply anywhere. As one planner put it, the test of a good street is simple: would you let a ten-year-old walk along it alone?
